definition: taking effect from a date in the past
memoryTip: Retro = back: the rule reaches backward in time.
correctPassage: The pay raise was retroactive to January, so employees received months of back pay.
wrongPassages: She preferred retroactive furniture that looked like it came from the 1950s.
The coach ran a retroactive drill so the team could practice the play again.
His retroactive mood made him refuse every new idea on principle.

definition: respond to a gesture or action with a corresponding one
memoryTip: Reciprocal: give back the same kind of gesture you got.
correctPassage: When one nation cut tariffs, trading partners were expected to reciprocate.
wrongPassages: He tried to reciprocate the broken vase by gluing the shards back together.
The engine will reciprocate fuel into electricity more efficiently this year.
She hoped to reciprocate her essay by cutting it from five pages to two.

definition: withdraw from involvement; detach
memoryTip: Dis + engage: unhook yourself and step away.
correctPassage: Mediators urged both armies to disengage and pull back from the border.
wrongPassages: The company planned to disengage three new factories next quarter.
She tried to disengage the audience by telling a long, lively story.
Judges will disengage the winner after scoring each routine.

definition: causing or likely to cause argument; quarrelsome
memoryTip: Full of contention — built to start a fight.
correctPassage: Land rights remain a contentious issue that splits the community.
wrongPassages: The museum display was contentious, packing a thousand years into one case.
Her contentious notes summarized every lecture in neat bullet points.
They chose a contentious hotel because it was quiet and inexpensive.

definition: open to more than one interpretation; ambiguous
memoryTip: Equi-vocal: equal voices, so the meaning cuts both ways.
correctPassage: His answer was deliberately equivocal, satisfying neither side completely.
wrongPassages: The coach was equivocal about practice, repeating the same drills every day.
She gave an equivocal speech praising the team without a single reservation.
The recipe was equivocal, listing exact grams for every ingredient.

definition: not clearly visible or attracting attention
memoryTip: In-conspicuous: the opposite of flashy — easy to miss.
correctPassage: The security camera is small enough to stay inconspicuous in the hallway.
wrongPassages: Her inconspicuous costume, covered in sequins, lit up the whole stage.
The billboard was inconspicuous, towering over the highway in neon.
He made an inconspicuous entrance by arriving with a marching band.

definition: combine two things into one, often mistakenly
memoryTip: Con-flate: fuse two ideas into one (sometimes wrongly).
correctPassage: Critics warned not to conflate correlation with causation in the study.
wrongPassages: Engineers will conflate the bridge by replacing every rusted bolt.
She tried to conflate the argument by calmly listing each side’s points.
The bank will conflate the loan so borrowers have more time to repay.

definition: build or form again from parts; restore
memoryTip: Re-constitute: put the pieces back together as a whole.
correctPassage: Add warm water to reconstitute the powdered soup before serving.
wrongPassages: The mayor vowed to reconstitute traffic by adding more stop signs downtown.
She will reconstitute the novel by cutting the final three chapters.
Judges reconstitute scores so the lowest mark automatically wins.

definition: lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
memoryTip: A-pathos: no feeling — you simply don’t care.
correctPassage: Voter apathy, not anger, explained the record-low turnout.
wrongPassages: Her apathy for the project showed in late nights and extra revisions.
The crowd’s apathy exploded into cheers when the underdog scored.
Doctors treated his apathy with ice packs and a compression bandage.

definition: unchanging over time; unable to be altered
memoryTip: Im-mutable: cannot mutate — locked in place forever.
correctPassage: In the model, physical constants are treated as immutable.
wrongPassages: Fashion is immutable, flipping styles every few seasons.
His immutable mood swung from joy to rage within an hour.
They kept an immutable schedule so meetings could move as needed.

definition: better or greater than all others of the same kind
memoryTip: No rival left standing — best of its kind.
correctPassage: The archive is unrivaled in its coverage of early print culture.
wrongPassages: The team’s unrivaled season ended with last place in the standings.
Her unrivaled cooking was so ordinary that guests left hungry.
They sought an unrivaled compromise that left both sides equally unhappy.

definition: come together from different directions toward one point
memoryTip: Con-verge: paths meet at the same spot.
correctPassage: Independent studies converge on the same conclusion about the drug.
wrongPassages: The two parties plan to converge and ignore each other entirely.
After the summit, the roads will converge so traffic has more routes out.
She hoped the rumors would converge before anyone could fact-check them.

definition: free from a constraint, difficulty, or entanglement
memoryTip: Ex-tricate: pull yourself free from a trap or mess.
correctPassage: Diplomats worked for months to extricate the hostages unharmed.
wrongPassages: She tried to extricate the salad by tossing in more dressing.
The bank will extricate the loan by charging a higher interest rate.
He hoped to extricate the celebration by inviting twice as many guests.

definition: instruction or guidance under a teacher or guardian
memoryTip: Tutor’s wing: learning under someone’s care and teaching.
correctPassage: Under her tutelage, the young violinist advanced with remarkable speed.
wrongPassages: The club’s tutelage banned anyone under eighteen from entering.
His tutelage of the room meant stacking chairs against the wall.
They measured the river’s tutelage after weeks of heavy rain.

definition: be an early sign or version of something later
memoryTip: Pre-figure: an early sketch of what is still to come.
correctPassage: Those early sketches already prefigure the building’s final silhouette.
wrongPassages: Accountants will prefigure the books after the audit finds errors.
She tried to prefigure the cake by adding more frosting on top.
The storm will prefigure once the clouds have completely cleared.

definition: establish so firmly that change becomes difficult
memoryTip: Dig a trench and stay put — hard to dig out later.
correctPassage: Long-running subsidies can entrench wasteful habits if never reviewed.
wrongPassages: Volunteers will entrench the park by clearing litter every weekend.
The chef hoped to entrench the sauce by thinning it with water.
Editors entrench articles so readers finish them in under a minute.

definition: lay down as a rule; authorize a treatment
memoryTip: Pre-scribe: write the rule or medicine ahead of time.
correctPassage: The guidelines prescribe at least thirty minutes of activity each day.
wrongPassages: The judge will prescribe the defendant from leaving the county.
She tried to prescribe the rumor before it spread any further.
Mechanics prescribe oil only after the engine has already seized.

definition: noticeable in an unwelcome or intrusive way
memoryTip: Ob-trude: sticks out where it doesn’t belong.
correctPassage: An obtrusive logo on the cover pulled attention from the photograph.
wrongPassages: The spy stayed obtrusive by wearing gray and avoiding eye contact.
Her obtrusive handwriting was so faint that graders needed a lamp.
They designed an obtrusive interface that hid every button until needed.

definition: having a mysterious or obscure meaning
memoryTip: Like a cryptogram — meaning locked behind a code.
correctPassage: The note was so cryptic that no one could decode its intent.
wrongPassages: Her cryptic instructions listed every step in numbered order.
The map was cryptic, with bold labels on every street and landmark.
He gave a cryptic speech that left no room for another interpretation.

definition: fill up again; restore a supply
memoryTip: Re-plenish: make full again after something is used up.
correctPassage: Heavy rains helped replenish the reservoirs after a dry summer.
wrongPassages: The editor will replenish the article by cutting half its length.
They hope to replenish traffic by closing two of the three lanes.
She replenished the debt by borrowing even more from the bank.
